sections.content:
Chapter 1: Population growth and economic development: Causes, consequences, and controversies.
Chapter 2: Population Compositions by Age and Sex
Chapter 3: Mortality Analysis
Chapter 4: Fertility Analysis
Chapter 5: Migration Analysis

The contents are well designed but may lack of depth. In the 5 chapters, the last one is the most important one (which is Prof. Ma's research interest). After this course, you will understand the demographic trends in China (and other developing countries), as well as the underlying reasons. You will have a big advantage if you learned some Economics and have some basic understanding of China's history (especially 1949-1992). If you are an Economic student, you will be familiar with some names in this course, e.g., G. S. Becker and J. R. Hicks. FYI: I major in MAEC and have got an A- in SOSC 1350 (Contemporary China: Continuity and Change).
sections.teaching:
Prof. Ma speaks slowly in his lectures and sometimes use Mandarin Chinese to facilitate his speech, and it may be a little bit difficult to focus on what he intends to talk as he digresses frequently. I agree with the previous comment that you should understand Mandarin Chinese to take this course. However, he is trying hard to use his own experience in explaining the historical incidents that have influenced the demographics in China. For example, he said his name 忠東 means 忠於毛澤東, which was a popular name in the early 1960s. He also recalled the fast on Tian'anmen Square in 1989 before the June 4th incident, where 沒有吃的，但是好多喝的，還有蜂王漿. It is really interesting to listen to these stories.

Prof. Ma will mention what is going to be tested in the exam, so it is useful to follow him during his lectures. The recordings will also be provided, so you can review the lectures before the final exam. Just pay attention that the quality of the recording may not be high enough that sometimes you cannot clearly hear him in the recordings. (Disclaimer: I do not guarantee that the recordings will be provided in the following semesters.)
sections.grading:
Components of Final Grade:
Attendance (in-class quizzes): 15%
Assignments: 27%
Class discussion: 3%
Final examination: 55%

In short: The final grade is not released, but I think the grading is fair (and perhaps better than most other UST courses). I get an A+ in this course, which is much beyond my expectation.

The attendance is recorded by 3 quizzes based on supplementary videos played in the last 30 minutes of some classes. Every quiz contains 4 MCQs with 1.5 points each, and you can get 1 point each even you choose the wrong answer. The final score is calculated by the best 3 out of 4 quizzes, and I think most of the students (including me) get full marks. However, the quizzes are a little bit tricky, so please spend some time on watching the videos during the lectures.

The assignments are composed of 2 problem sets with calculations. The problem sets are not difficult at all, and everyone gets high marks (median 95/100 and 88/100 for the 2 problem sets). The TAs also provide detailed feedback to the assignments. Nevertheless, I strongly recommend you to read thoroughly through the problem sets before doing the calculation parts. My overall score is around the median (99/100, 85/100) due to some careless mistakes in the second problem set.

Class discussion is also encouraged, especially raising questions during the lecture breaks. Each time a student asks or answers a question, Prof. Ma will record their participation number. Even though some students (like me) keep asking silly questions, Prof. Ma will happily answer them. I guess each record accounts for 1% of the total score, while the maximum is 3%. If this is true, I get full marks in this part.

The final examination is a 3-hour closed book exam. There are 35 MCQs (around 49%), 1 calculation problem (around 11%), and 2 short essay problems (around 40%). The scores are not disclosed. The time is fairly enough for the problems, so please write carefully to make sure you get all key points.
sections.workload: The workload is quite light. You only need to go to the lectures (or do other things during the lectures and spend 2 days to go through the recordings) to have fair understanding of the materials. There are 2 problem sets, and each problem set takes around 2-3 hours to finish. Compared to other CCCs with essays or group projects, this course is definitely a smart choice.

sections.content:
To be frank, only 5 PowerPoint slides throughout the whole semester, namely:

1. Population Growth
- introduced basic concepts on population calculation and growth models
- poverty cycle

2. Population Composition
- Age groups, age structures
- Dependent Ratio
- Population pyramids
- Sex composition
- Demographic Transition

3. Mortality Analysis
- most important!! -> difference between crude death rate (CDR) and Age-adjusted death rate (ASDR)
- mortality trends

4. Fertility Analysis
- similar to Mortality, need to calculate the crude birth rate and standardized birth rate using age group

5. Migration analysis
- a lot of models
-Lewis model
- Stark Model
- Social Capital Theory
- Institutional Theory
- some trends and patterns

sections.content:
This course aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of population growth, distribution, composition, major demographic processes and their relationship with economic development. Special attention is given to the demographic trends and policies in both the Chinese Mainland and Hong Kong SAR. Basic concepts of economics and knowledge of development in the region are required for the exams. Students are assessed according to their performance in the final exam, assignments, random quizs and class discussion.

Course Structure
1. Population Growth and Economic Development: Causes, Consequences, and Controversies
2. Population Composition by Age and Sex: Marriage Squeeze and Population Aging
3. Fertility Analysis: Trends, Levels and Explanations
4. Migration: Explanation and Evaluation of Its Impact
5. Mortality Analysis: Causes, Epidemiological Transition, and Differentials in Mortality
6. Population Distribution: Urban and Regional Growth (optional)
sections.teaching:
Professor Ma teaches very well and often says "OK". He is a very kind teacher, and the TAs are also competent.
This semester, we have online classes on Zoom, and Professor Ma is very active in answering student questions. The class lasts a long time, but there are breaks in between.

He does not speak Mandarin very often during class and usually repeats what he says in English, so there is no problem for non-Mandarin speakers to attend the class. As long as you can memorize the PPTs (which are in English), you can even get a good grade without understanding what is being taught in class. There are no recordings to watch, but there are recordings(audio) to listen to.

====================================

马老师教得挺好的，经常说OK。很和善的老师，TA也称职。
我们这学期是zoom上课，马老师回答学生问题很积极。一整节课上下来时间很长，但是中间会给休息的时间。
上课说得普通话其实不多，而且都又讲了一遍英文。不存在说听不懂中文就上不了课的程度。
没有recording看，但是有录音可以听。

sections.workload:
The course is still quite relaxed. Class participation is required through class discussions, and during the Zoom period, the number of times a student speaks is counted, so just repeat the answers along with other classmates.
The quizzes are multiple-choice questions based on the videos shown in class. If you listen carefully, you will be able to answer them.
The two assignments consist of calculation questions and short answer questions, and you need to use Word to create statistical charts, which are similar to the problem sets in the Business School (I am from the School of Engineering).

During the last class, Professor Ma will discuss the exam points for the final exam, so it is important to take notes and review them.
However, I memorized all of the lecture notes, including the various charts and data, and did well on the final exam. Therefore, memorizing more will earn you more points, and if you memorize enough, you will get a good grade.

In my personal opinion, the content of the lecture notes was covered in the final exam, and the short essay questions were quite objective. Simply reiterating the theoretical content from the PPT is enough, and there is no need to write a lot of your own thoughts.

I did not feel that there was any fierce competition with students from SHSS, it's not that hard :)

====================================

还是很轻松的，上课需要参与课堂讨论，zoom时期就是统计发言次数，跟着其他同学一起复读答案就可以。

Quiz是单选题，上课看视频，回答几个视频中提到答案的问题，基本上听了就会做。

两个assignment都是计算题和简答题，需要拿word做统计图，和商院那些problem set有点像（我本人是工院的）。

最后一节课马老师会讲期末考试的考点，都记下来复习就行。

sections.content:
This course is mainly about the modern population development of China from around the 1950s till the present. There are some calculations such as population and fertility rate, which you have to memorize the theories and formulas in the final exam.  

Course Structure

1. Population Growth and Economic Development: Causes, Consequences, and Controversies
2. Population Composition by Age and Sex: Marriage Squeeze and Population Aging
3. Fertility Analysis: Trends, Levels and Explanations
4. Migration: Explanation and Evaluation of Its Impact
5. Mortality Analysis: Causes, Epidemiological Transition, and Differentials in Mortality
6. Population Distribution: Urban and Regional Growth (optional)
sections.teaching: The course is a 3-hour lecture every week. The professor was good at explaining the facts and sometimes would tell us about his past in China. But I often dozed off during his lectures, as his voice sounds like he is mumbling. He sometimes also uses mandarin and Chinese characters to explain some terminology, so non-local students have to bear this in mind.
sections.grading:
Assignment (2)         22%
Class attendance & Quizs  (5)     15%
Final Exam (MC, Calculation, essay Qs) 60%
Discussion (answering professor's questions or asking him questions during breaks)               3%

The assignments are not hard as most of the answers can be found in the slide, but you have elaborate on them and do multiple calculations. Most importantly, the grade heavily depends on the final exam.

I got A- for my final grade. Both of my assignments are above the mean by 4 to 5 marks. The mark for final exam was unreleased.
sections.workload: There are 2 assignments and in-class quizzes about the videos which the TA plays. So be sure to attend classes as the in-class quizzes are randomly released after the professor's lecture.

This semester is special. Due to the suspension of classes, he canceled the second assignment and the upcoming quizzes, so the percentage of final increases from 45% to 60%.

The first assignment is easy, just some high school maths. Just be careful about which formula has to be used.

I suggest you attend all the lectures because it has pop-up quizzes, but the quizzes are at the end of the lecture. Quizzes are not related to the lecture notes, the questions are based on the video played by the TA, easy questions and almost everyone got full mark. Not need to revise for the quizzes.

The midterm is around 20MCs, one short essay question. The final is open book only for this semester. Similar to midterm, Mcs and one short essay question. I think the difficulty for the final is lower than the previous regular semester, just for this semester.

He provided lecture videos (but I think just for this semester because those videos only covered materials after suspension of classes). I watched them all before the final exams, 6 hours in total, extra 2 hours to revise, then A range.

sections.grading:

* if you listen carefully in class and do not skip lectures, it doesn't take you that much time to revise for final

One of my groupmate got A while another got C+

* MCQs include presentation materials from other groups with 1 question from each group (total 14 groups)
